stories.title: Three Votes for a Hike Shift the Fed’s Center of Gravity: Analysis
stories.excerpt: The Federal Reserve left its benchmark interest rate unchanged at 3.50% to 3.75% on Wednesday, extending its policy pause for a fifth consecutive meeting while delivering a clear signal that the debate inside the central bank has become increasingly hawkish.  Although the decision was largely anticipated, the meeting was marked by a rare three-way dissent from Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, Minneapolis Fed President Neel Kashkari and Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan, who each favored raising rates by 25 basis points. It was the first time since 2016 that three Federal Open Market Committee members dissented in the same direction on a policy decision, suggesting momentum is building toward tightening should inflation remain stubborn.  Another Pause, But Not a Pivot Market strategists said investors should not mistake Warsh’s decision as dovish. “The Fed’s decision to hold rates steady this week was our base case, but this was not a typical hold,” Juan Xavier Sánchez, head of wealth strategy at Activest Wealth Management, told Connect Money. “We said when Chairman Warsh took over that markets should prepare for more volatility as the Fed becomes less predictable, and that is exactly what is playing out.”  Sánchez said the three dissents reinforce the committee’s increasingly hawkish bias and could strengthen Chair Kevin Warsh’s efforts to contain inflation expectations.  Despite the uncertainty, he remains constructive on markets. “Corporate earnings have been resilient, and markets can absorb a less predictable Fed as long as earnings hold up,” Sánchez said. “The lesson of this year is simple: portfolios should be built to work whether the Fed hikes or holds, not on guessing the Fed correctly.”  Energy Risks Keep Inflation in Focus The Fed’s challenge has become increasingly compl
bullets: Fed held rates at 3.50–3.75%, but three FOMC members dissented in favor of 25bp hike.
First three-way dissent since 2016 signals hawkish momentum if inflation remains sticky.
Chair Warsh reinforces 2% inflation target as chief goal; credibility rests on commitment.
stories.summary: The Federal Reserve held its benchmark rate steady at 3.50–3.75% for the fifth consecutive meeting, but the decision carried a rare three-way dissent from regional Fed presidents favoring a 25 basis point increase. This is the first time since 2016 that three FOMC members dissented in the same direction, signaling rising internal pressure to tighten if inflation doesn't cool. Chair Kevin Warsh stated the Fed will not waver from its 2% inflation target and that five years of above-target inflation cannot be cured quickly.
stories.impact: The hawkish dissent and Warsh's rigid commitment to inflation targeting suggest cap rates and financing costs may not ease as quickly as some developers have priced into underwriting. While rates are on hold today, the institutional shift toward tightening means multifamily development pro formas should assume rate risk remains elevated through 2025; refinance and construction loan availability could tighten if inflation data surprises to the upside, compressing returns on new starts and lengthening hold periods for value-add plays.

stories.title: NY Investor Snags First Folsom Apartments on Market in Four Years
stories.excerpt: CBRE arranged the sale of Talavera, a 293-unit apartment community in Folsom, to New York-based Sentinel Real Estate. Talavera was the first asset to become available in the Folsom submarket in four years. CBRE’s Marc Ross, Eli Hanacek, Joe McNamara and Claire Holt represented the sellers, USA Properties & Strand Financial. Pricing was not disclosed. “Talavera is the most compelling institutional multifamily opportunity to emerge in the Sacramento region in 20+ years, anchored by its coveted position in the Folsom submarket,” said Ross. “Top of the market demographics and schools, strong employment growth, high barriers to new construction, and exceptional location fundamentals have sustained deep investor demand, and Talavera is exceptionally well-positioned to capitalize on all of them.” Located at 1550 Broadstone Pkwy, the four-building community was built in 2020. Talavera is Folsom’s only elevator-served multifamily property. The property was 96% occupied at the time of sale. The post NY Investor Snags First Folsom Apartments on Market in Four Years appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Sentinel Real Estate (NYC) acquired Talavera, 293-unit Folsom, CA apartment; first submarket sale in 4 years.
Property built 2020, 96% occupied, only elevator-served multifamily in Folsom; strong employment and schools.
High barriers to new construction and deep investor demand sustain prices despite supply drought.
stories.summary: A New York-based investor, Sentinel Real Estate, purchased Talavera, a 293-unit multifamily community in Folsom, California, marking the first major apartment transaction in the submarket in four years. Built in 2020 and 96% leased at time of sale, Talavera is the only elevator-served apartment property in Folsom and sits on a coveted site near strong employment hubs and top-tier schools. The Folsom submarket boasts high barriers to new construction and has sustained deep institutional investor demand.
stories.impact: The four-year supply drought and institutional rush into a 293-unit asset signals severe undersupply in the Folsom/Sacramento corridor and validates rent growth tailwinds. The lack of new construction (high barriers) and strong employment fundamentals create a window for Trammell Crow to identify and acquire development sites in Folsom or nearby suburban Sacramento submarkets before competition intensifies; the Sentinel deal proves institutional capital is hungry for any quality product, supporting aggressive underwriting on new starts.

stories.title: Friedman Real Completes Sale of Virginia Technology Center for $13M

Friedman represented the seller, a private investor, in the transaction. The buyer, Cove Capital, purchased the property for $13.4 million. Brian Brockman of Bang Realty was the in-state broker.Built in 1986, the property is situated on a site spanning more than six acres. The center also includes 370 parking spaces. stories.title: MassDevelopment Launches “Creative District” Pilot Program in North Adams
stories.excerpt: MassDevelopment on Wednesday announced an economic development pilot program in North Adams that will leverage arts and culture as drivers of growth while strengthening downtown revitalization efforts, supporting small businesses and creative entrepreneurs, and positioning the Northern Berkshires for future public and private investment. Funded by a $2.5-million Barr Foundation grant, the “Creative District” pilot program will run for three years. Through this pilot program, North Adams will be supported by a Creative District fellow, a full-time MassDevelopment employee who will work alongside local partners. The pilot program will also provide North Adams with access to a range of tools including technical assistance, flexible funding, and integrated arts and culture planning. “North Adams has built a strong identity around arts, culture, and creativity, making it a destination that attracts visitors, supports local businesses, and strengthens the regional economy,” said Economic Development Secretary Eric Paley, who serves as Chair of MassDevelopment’s Board of Directors. “This partnership with the Barr Foundation builds on those strengths by providing the resources, expertise, and local capacity to help the community grow while preserving what makes North Adams unique.” The post MassDevelopment Launches “Creative District” Pilot Program in North Adams appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: MassDevelopment launches $2.5M 'Creative District' pilot in North Adams, MA for 3 years.
Program funds arts/culture-led downtown revitalization, small business support, and creative entrepreneur ecosystem.
Positioning Northern Berkshires for future public and private investment via placemaking.
stories.summary: MassDevelopment, with $2.5 million in Barr Foundation funding, announced a three-year "Creative District" pilot program in North Adams, Massachusetts aimed at leveraging arts and culture as economic drivers. The program will employ a dedicated Creative District fellow and provide technical assistance, flexible funding, and integrated arts and culture planning to strengthen downtown revitalization and support creative entrepreneurs. North Adams has an existing strong identity around arts, culture, and creativity.
stories.impact: Arts-led downtown revitalization programs create demand-side tailwinds for multifamily near cultural anchors; North Adams' focus on placemaking and small-business support can stabilize and grow the renter base over three years. Developers should monitor North Adams for emerging mixed-use or transit-oriented apartment opportunities tied to cultural programming and lower construction costs relative to Boston metros; the program signals city-backed stabilization that reduces downside risk on speculative residential infill.

stories.title: CenterSquare Acquires Geneva Commons Retail Center
stories.excerpt: CenterSquare has acquired a significant portion of Geneva Commons, adding the property to its essential service retail portfolio. Geneva Commons is located along Randall Road, and the center includes over 80 retailers and restaurants spread over 418,000 square feet. CenterSquare purchased six buildings totaling 87,649 square feet within the lifestyle destination. The latest addition brings the company’s portfolio to 81 acquisitions nationally.Geneva Commons is located in a dominant retail corridor with high visibility, and the property is 97% leased. Lamar Companies, in conjunction with Real Capital Solutions, acquired Geneva Commons for $63.8 million, down from the $124.5 million the seller, LaSalle Investment Management, paid for it in 2013. Lamar has invested over $2.4 million in capital improvements following the acquisition. The shopping center has seen continued leasing activity, recently signing 45,951 square feet of new retail and restaurant leases with new tenants including Lululemon, Warby Parker, Big Blue Swim School, Club Champion, Vera Bradley and Miniso. The post CenterSquare Acquires Geneva Commons Retail Center appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: CenterSquare acquired six buildings totaling 87,649 sf within Geneva Commons retail, Randall Road, Chicago.
Center is 97% leased with 80+ retailers; recent leases include Lululemon, Warby Parker, Club Champion.
Transaction does not involve multifamily residential.
stories.summary: CenterSquare acquired six buildings comprising 87,649 square feet within Geneva Commons, a 418,000-square-foot lifestyle destination retail center along Randall Road in Chicago. The property is 97% leased and recently signed 45,951 square feet of new retail and restaurant leases. CenterSquare's acquisition adds to its national essential-service retail portfolio.
stories.impact: Not directly relevant to multifamily development; this is a retail-focused transaction. However, the strong leasing momentum and high occupancy at a major retail center suggest robust consumer spending and foot traffic in the Chicago Randall Road corridor, which could support mixed-use or nearby multifamily demand.

stories.title: City Selects Slate Property Group, Hudson Companies to Build 980 Homes in LIC
stories.excerpt: A development team made up of Slate Property Group, Hudson Companies and Volunteers of America has been chosen to create nearly 1,000 new homes upon a vacant parcel in Long Island City, Queens. The 70,000-square-foot development, at 54-42 Second Street, will be called the Orion, and two-thirds of its units will be set aside as affordable housing. “It is exactly what New York needs,” David Schwartz, principal and co-founder of Slate Property Group, said in a statement. “And we look forward to working with City Hall to get shovels in the ground as soon as possible.” The parcel sits within the 30-acre Hunter’s Point South housing complex. When completed, Hunter’s Point South is expected to feature approximately 5,000 new homes, roughly 3,000 of which will be affordable. The city’s Department of Housing Preservation and Development (HPD) began courting developers for the site, known as Parcel E, in June of last year. The request for proposals came with the requirement that Parcel E host more affordable homes than previous phases. The Orion will include approximately 980 new apartments. Two-thirds of the apartments, roughly 658 units, will be income-restricted, affordable to extremely low- to moderate-income households. Approximately 150 units will be set aside as supportive apartments. “Reaching households at every income level in a high-opportunity neighborhood like Hunter’s Point reflects a simple belief: Where New Yorkers live shouldn’t come down to income alone,” said Laszlo Syrop, principal and head of acquisitions at Hudson Companies. The mixed-use community, designed by Marvel Architects, will feature an affordable child care center, a workforce development center and a community pool. Approximately 6,000 square feet of ground-floor commercial retail space will also be made available along Second Street and Center Boulevard. bullets: Slate Property Group, Hudson Companies, Volunteers of America selected to develop 980 units at 54-42 Second Street, Long Island City, Queens.
Two-thirds (650+ units) set aside as affordable housing; part of 30-acre Hunter's Point South complex.
Hunter's Point South targeting ~5,000 total new homes (3,000 affordable) when fully built out.
stories.summary: A development team led by Slate Property Group and Hudson Companies has been selected to build "The Orion," a new 980-unit apartment community at 54-42 Second Street in Long Island City, Queens. Two-thirds of the units will be affordable housing. The development sits within the 30-acre Hunter's Point South housing complex, which is expected to deliver approximately 5,000 new homes (roughly 3,000 affordable) upon completion. The city's HPD released the parcel for RFP in June of the prior year.
stories.impact: Hunter's Point South represents a rare, large-scale, city-backed residential pipeline in Queens with strong affordability mandates and public transit access (Metrorail). The 5,000-unit phase-out signals sustained demand-side growth in Long Island City and Queens; Trammell Crow should monitor adjacent or nearby parcels for market-rate or mixed-income opportunities as Hunter's Point South buildout progresses, as the project will anchor renter population and employment density in the waterfront corridor, creating secondary development opportunity windows.

stories.title: AI Infrastructure Firm Treeswift Signs 7K-SF Lease at 256 West 38th Street
stories.excerpt: An artificial intelligence-driven infrastructure technology company is relocating its offices to Midtown. Philadelphia-based Treeswift signed a four-year, 7,487-square-foot lease on the entire 11th floor of the Hakimian Organization’s 256 West 38th Street in an expansion of its New York City operations, according to landlord broker Lee & Associates NYC. Asking rent was $39 per square foot. It is unclear where Treeswift is relocating from within New York City, but the company also has an office in Philadelphia. “Artificial intelligence companies have become one of the most active drivers of office leasing demand in Manhattan, but they are not all looking for trophy towers,” Lee & Associates’ Todd Korren, who represented the landlord alongside Noah Caspi, said in a statement. “As these businesses grow, they are seeking efficient, well-connected headquarters that support collaboration, attract talent and provide long-term value. Treeswift’s relocation reflects that trend.” Daniel Rodriguez Sains of Buchbinder Warren negotiated on behalf of the tenant and did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Treeswift specializes in helping clients with infrastructure inspections, vegetation management, construction planning, wildfire mitigation and storm response, according to the brokerage. The firm will move into its new offices at 256 West 38th Street in August. It’s unclear when the Rex Hakimian-led firm got involved in the building’s ownership, but his name starts showing up on deed filings sometime after March 2025, when Empire Capital Holdings acquired the property and nearby 229 West 36th Street in a state of distress for a steep discount at $50 million. The seller, Investcorp, purchased the two buildings for $157 million in 2017, Commercial Observer previously reported. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Treeswift (Philadelphia-based AI infrastructure firm) signed 7,487-sf lease, 256 West 38th Street, Midtown Manhattan.
Four-year lease at $39/sf; entire 11th floor; company expanding NYC operations.
AI companies increasingly active office tenants; seeking efficient, collaborative space, not trophy towers.
stories.summary: Philadelphia-based Treeswift, an AI-driven infrastructure technology company, signed a four-year lease for 7,487 square feet on the 11th floor of 256 West 38th Street in Midtown Manhattan at $39 per square foot. The deal reflects Treeswift's expansion of New York City operations. Brokers note that AI companies have become major drivers of office leasing in Manhattan but are increasingly seeking efficient, well-connected headquarters over trophy tower space.
stories.impact: Not directly relevant to multifamily, but the AI company expansion in Midtown signals strong talent attraction and job creation in technology sectors, which should drive renter demand for apartments near Midtown corridors. Multifamily developers should note that Midtown's office leasing strength supports sustained demand for rental housing; younger, higher-income tech workers relocating or expanding NYC presence support premium studio and one-bedroom rents near transit to tech hubs.

stories.title: PCCP, Stonemont Close on $1B-Plus Acquisition of Blackstone Industrial Portfolio
stories.excerpt: PCCP and Stonemont Financial Group are officially the new owners of a 5.9 million-square-foot industrial portfolio, Commercial Observer can first report. The joint venture acquired the 38 assets, located across 14 markets in 10 states, for upward of $1 billion with Blackstone as the seller, according to an article from Real Estate Alert preceding the sale. The portfolio was sold via an off-market transaction, with Eastdil Secured serving as adviser, and the transaction closed July 29. It wasn’t immediately clear how the acquisition was financed. “The acquisition of this portfolio represents PCCP’s continued conviction in the industrial sector and in markets we have actively invested in within the last five years,” Ryan Dodge, a partner with PCCP, said. “We believe our industrial portfolio continues to exhibit strong momentum, with increased leasing demand in recent months. In our view, this portfolio is well positioned to benefit from those same market tailwinds.” The portfolio — leased to a diverse roster of more than 70 tenants — is located across infill submarkets, including Denver, Dallas, Atlanta, and Charlotte, N.C., as well as strong growth markets like San Diego, Reno, Nev., and El Paso, Texas. With PCCP and Stonemount Financial now in the driver’s seat, the JV’s plan is to focus on revenue growth via contractual rent increases and marking-to-market on leases that are being renewed, according to a release. “This transaction reflects our conviction in the long-term fundamentals of the industrial real estate sector,” said Zack Markwell, CEO and managing principal at Stonemont. “We are pleased to have once again partnered with PCCP and will continue to pursue attractive acquisition opportunities alongside our active development program.” The industrial sector is one of PCCP’s investment fortés, with the firm currently managing more than 68 million square feet of industrial assets over 52 markets. This acquisition brings its count to 262 industrial transactions.
bullets: PCCP and Stonemont acquired 5.9M-sf industrial portfolio (38 assets, 14 markets, 10 states) from Blackstone for $1B+.
Portfolio well-leased; closed July 29 off-market via Eastdil; reflects conviction in industrial sector tailwinds.
Transaction does not involve multifamily residential.
stories.summary: PCCP and Stonemont Financial Group closed the acquisition of a 5.9 million-square-foot industrial portfolio comprising 38 assets across 14 markets in 10 states from Blackstone for over $1 billion. The off-market transaction closed July 29 with Eastdil Secured serving as adviser. The portfolio is well-leased and the buyers cited strong momentum in industrial leasing demand.
stories.impact: Not directly relevant to multifamily development; this is an industrial/logistics transaction. However, the billion-dollar capital redeployment from Blackstone into industrial signals fund-level conviction in logistics and supply-chain real estate, potentially indicating capital is rotated away from other property types; monitoring institutional capital flows helps Trammell Crow understand relative appetite for multifamily debt and equity in the current cycle.

stories.title: Fed Holds Interest Rates in Warsh’s Second Meeting as FOMC Chair
stories.excerpt: The second Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting under new Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh signaled another reality check of higher-for-longer interest rates to the commercial real estate industry. In a 9-3 vote, the FOMC maintained its benchmark interest rate Wednesday at between 3.5 percent and 3.75 percent for the fifth straight meeting, citing inflation risks from ongoing war in Iran. Inflation remains well above the Fed’s 2 percent target at a time when Warsh has laid the groundwork for possibly changing its data approach when crafting monetary policy decisions. Warsh said in a post-meeting press conference that the FOMC doesn’t have a “soft target” for inflation and remains committed to the 2 percent annual rate as a chief goal. “We have begun a new chapter and we understand that the five-plus years of inflation above target cannot be cured in nine weeks or by a single month of modest price decreases,” Warsh said. “This Fed will not waver. Our credibility rests on performing our duties and delivering on our responsibilities.” The vote to maintain interest rates came with some dissent as FOMC regional presidents Beth M. Hammack of Cleveland, Neel Kashkari of Minneapolis and Lorie K. Logan of Dallas voted no, preferring instead to implement a quarter-point hike. Warsh’s second meeting leading the Fed after replacing Jerome Powell as chair in May occurred two weeks after he said during congressional testimony that the FOMC has “no tolerance for persistently elevated inflation.” Warsh also spoke to whether traditional inflation gauges such as the Consumer Price Index and the Producer Price Index (PPI) should be rethought. The new Fed chair appointed a task force in June that will examine whether the central bank’s long-standing inflation metrics needs to change, with findings expected later in the year. bullets: Fed maintained 3.5–3.75% rate in 9-3 vote; three members dissented in favor of hike.
Chair Warsh reaffirms no 'soft target' for 2% inflation; will not waver despite five years above target.
Inflation remains well above 2% target; higher-for-longer rate backdrop persists.
stories.summary: In Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's second FOMC meeting, the committee voted 9-3 to maintain the benchmark interest rate at 3.5–3.75% for the fifth consecutive meeting. Three regional Fed presidents dissented in favor of a 25 basis point increase, citing inflation risks. Warsh stated in his post-meeting press conference that the Fed has no "soft target" for inflation and remains committed to the 2% annual rate, acknowledging that five-plus years of above-target inflation cannot be cured in nine weeks.
stories.impact: Duplicate of article #1 with slightly different framing. The message is consistent: rates staying elevated, hawkish dissent rising, and Warsh's hard line on inflation signal extended higher-rate environment. Multifamily underwriting should assume cap rates remain compressed relative to long-term averages; debt service on new construction and refinance will remain elevated, pressuring yields and extending hold periods. Construction financing availability may tighten if inflation data remains sticky, forcing Trammell Crow to lock in construction debt early and prioritize shovel-ready sites.

stories.title: Madison Realty Capital Leads $227M Refi of New Miami-Dade Rental
stories.excerpt: Baron Property Group (BPG) has secured $226.5 million to refinance a newly completed multifamily development in Hialeah, Fla. Madison Realty Capital and Yellowstone Real Estate provided the debt backing the 559-unit Metro Parc at 955 East 25th Street, about a block west of Metrorail and Tri-Rail transfer stations in a working-class area of Miami-Dade County. BPG completed the 10-story building last year after securing a $148 million construction loan from Post Road Group in 2022. The 754,016-square-foot project — which includes 15,000 square feet of retail space, partly leased to Cuban bakery Mr. Baker — is nearly 50 percent leased, according to a representative for the developer. The refinance will replace the project’s construction loan and will serve as a bridge to permanent financing. Ben Suky brokered the transaction. Metro Parc represents the first phase of Baron Property Group’s 2.3 million-square-foot residential development. The second phase, called Metro Parc North and adjacent to Metro Parc, recently topped out and is scheduled to be completed in late 2027. Post Road Group provided a $206 million construction loan for that phase last year. MG Developer, an original partner in both Metro Parc projects, is no longer involved, per a representative for BPG, who has not provided additional details. MG Developer is currently building the 347-unit Metro Parc South across the street after landing a $105 million construction loan last year. Julia Echikson can be reached at jechikson@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Baron Property Group refinanced Metro Parc, 559 units in Hialeah, FL for $226.5M via Madison Realty Capital.
Nearly 50% leased post-completion; replaced $148M construction loan from 2022; bridge to permanent financing.
First phase of 2.3M-sf development; second phase (Metro Parc North) recently topped out.
stories.summary: Baron Property Group secured a $226.5 million refinance from Madison Realty Capital and Yellowstone Real Estate for Metro Parc, a newly completed 559-unit, 10-story apartment development in Hialeah, Florida near Metrorail and Tri-Rail stations. The property, completed last year after a $148 million construction loan from Post Road Group in 2022, is nearly 50% leased and includes 15,000 square feet of retail (including a Cuban bakery). The refinance replaces the construction loan and serves as a bridge to permanent financing. Metro Parc is the first phase of Baron's 2.3 million-square-foot residential development; phase two (Metro Parc North) recently topped out.
stories.impact: Successful refi of a newly completed multifamily asset in Hialeah signals that lenders (Madison, Yellowstone) are confident in Miami-Dade demand and willing to extend bridge financing into permanent structures. However, the 50% lease-up suggests slower stabilization; Trammell Crow should note that South Florida lease-up timelines may be lengthening due to higher rents and elevated rates affecting tenant absorption. The massive development pipeline (2.3M sf residential) in Metro Parc's corridor could signal potential supply overhang; developers should stress-test pro formas for longer lease-up, higher concessions, and downward rent pressure in the Hialeah submarket as competing supply delivers.
